title: Narrowing the funnel
sub: Twelve independent runs of each estimator. Same cost, very different spread.

frames.caption: Estimate E[e<sup>U</sup>] for U uniform on [0, 1] by averaging samples. The true answer is e − 1 ≈ 1.718 (dashed). Each blue line is one independent run's running average.
The runs drift towards the answer, but they disagree. The thin grey curves are ±2 standard errors: about 95% of runs should sit inside them.
The funnel narrows like 1/√n. Halving the spread takes four times as many samples.
After 200 samples the runs still disagree in the second decimal place. Every technique in this post is a way of making this funnel narrower for the same number of samples.
Antithetic pairs: draw u, and also use 1 − u. When e<sup>u</sup> is high, e<sup>1−u</sup> is low, so each pair's average is already close to the answer.
The same number of function evaluations as the plain runs, but the funnel is far narrower.
e<sup>u</sup> is monotone, so the pair is negatively correlated, and the variance drops by a factor of about 31.
One line of code, and the error is 6 times smaller than plain Monte Carlo at the same cost. The flat steps are because the estimate only moves once per pair.

Control variate: use g(U) = U, whose mean we know is ½, and average e<sup>U</sup> − c(U − ½). The correction is zero on average, so the estimate stays unbiased. With c = Cov/Var ≈ 1.69 it cancels most of the noise.
U and e<sup>U</sup> have correlation 0.99. Whatever error U makes, e<sup>U</sup> makes nearly the same one, and the subtraction removes it.
The variance is 1 − ρ² of the original: about 1/62.
The same idea, with the value function as g, is the baseline in policy gradients.

A rare event: how likely is a standard normal to exceed 4? The answer is 3.17 in 100,000 (dashed). Grey: 12 plain Monte Carlo runs. Blue: 12 runs that sample from N(4, 1) instead and reweight each sample by p(x)/q(x).
Plain sampling has seen no event at all, so it estimates exactly zero. Importance sampling puts half its samples in the region that matters, and the weights correct for the distortion.

All 12 plain runs are still at zero. Had one been lucky, a single hit in 800 samples would put its estimate at 125 in 100,000: forty times too high. Plain sampling of a rare event is either zero or wildly wrong.

After 2,000 samples the importance-sampled runs agree to within about 5%. Plain Monte Carlo would need over ten million samples to do as well. The catch: the proposal must cover wherever p·f is large, or a few huge weights take over.
